name: Mt. Rainier
whyNotable: Most glaciated peak in the Lower 48 — a serious glacier climb, not a walk-up.
description: Mount Rainier is the most glaciated peak in the contiguous United States. Standard routes (DC, Emmons) are glacier climbs with crevasse hazard, party travel, and overnight high camps. Stage from Ashford / Paradise, carry a climbing pass, and treat weather and seracs as trip-ending risks—not scenery.

name: Mt. Shasta
whyNotable: A lone Cascade volcano over northern California — Avalanche Gulch is the classic snow climb.
description: Mount Shasta rises alone above the Shasta Valley. Avalanche Gulch from Bunny Flat is the standard snow/glacier route: early season snow travel, red-fir / Helen Lake camps, and a summit plateau with big weather. A USFS summit pass is required above 10,000 ft. Stage in the town of Mount Shasta and watch spring avalanche conditions.

name: Lassen Peak
whyNotable: California’s southern Cascade volcano and a classic national-park summit hike.
description: Southernmost Cascade volcano and the high point of Lassen Volcanic National Park — a popular summer trail to a cratered summit above Lake Helen.

name: San Jacinto Peak
whyNotable: One of Southern California’s most prominent peaks and a classic Palm Springs tram-to-summit hike.
description: Southern California sky-island summit above Palm Springs — tram-accessible wilderness with steep trails from Long Valley to a granite high point.

name: San Gorgonio Mountain
whyNotable: Southern California’s high point and a rite-of-passage San Bernardino wilderness hike.
description: Highest peak in Southern California — a long wilderness hike via Vivian Creek or other San Gorgonio Wilderness trails above Forest Falls.

name: Mt. San Antonio
whyNotable: The iconic San Gabriel high point and one of the most climbed peaks in Southern California.
description: Mt. Baldy — Los Angeles’s backyard 10,000-footer via Baldy Bowl, Ski Hut, or Devil’s Backbone routes in Angeles National Forest.

name: Mt. Hood
whyNotable: Oregon’s classic Cascade snow climb above Timberline — popular, crevassed, and weather-volatile.
description: Mount Hood’s south-side routes from Timberline Lodge are the Pacific Northwest’s most popular snow climbs. Expect early alpine starts, steep snow, and bergschrund / rock-fall hazard near the Pearly Gates or Old Chute. No general climbing permit, but avalanche and spring weather end seasons fast. Stage in Government Camp.

name: South Sister
whyNotable: Highest peak in Oregon’s Cascades and the most climbed Oregon volcano.
description: Oregon’s highest Cascade volcano and the state’s most popular high summit hike — a long climber’s trail from the Devils Lake / Green Lakes area near Bend.

name: North Sister
whyNotable: Hardest of the Three Sisters; classic Oregon Cascade technical summit.
description: The oldest and most eroded of Oregon’s Three Sisters — a technical Cascade climb of rotten volcanic rock, far harder than South Sister.

name: Middle Sister
whyNotable: Central Three Sisters summit; popular Oregon Cascade alpine day climb.
description: The middle peak of Oregon’s Three Sisters — a moderate snow and scree climb often done as a long day from the Pole Creek or Obsidian approaches.

name: Mt. Jefferson
whyNotable: Oregon’s #2 Cascade summit and a committing wilderness climb north of the Three Sisters.
description: Oregon’s second-highest Cascade volcano — a remote, technical summit north of Sisters with long approaches through Jefferson Wilderness.

name: Broken Top
whyNotable: Signature Central Oregon volcano and a favorite scramble above the Green Lakes basin.
description: Jagged Cascade volcano beside the Three Sisters — popular Green Lakes and No Name Lake approaches with a scramble summit in Deschutes National Forest.

name: Mt. Baker
whyNotable: The northernmost Cascade volcano in the contiguous U.S.
description: The northernmost Cascade volcano in the contiguous U.S., heavily glaciated and a classic Pacific Northwest ski-mountaineering objective.

name: Glacier Peak
whyNotable: One of the major Cascade stratovolcanoes and Washington’s most remote high volcano.
description: Washington’s remote Cascade volcano east of Darrington — a long wilderness approach to glaciers and a classic Pacific Northwest mountaineering objective.

name: Mt. Stuart
whyNotable: Highest non-volcanic peak in Washington; landmark of the Enchantments.
description: The non-volcanic king of the central Washington Cascades — a massive granite massif with classic alpine rock routes above the Enchantments.

name: Mt. Shuksan
whyNotable: One of the most photographed mountains in the Cascades; classic alpine climbing above Baker Lake country.
description: Iconic North Cascades pyramid above Artist Point and Picture Lake — a photogenic alpine peak and classic mountaineering objective near Mt. Baker.

name: Mt. Olympus
whyNotable: Signature summit of Olympic National Park and Washington’s wet-side alpine icon.
description: The glaciated high point of Olympic National Park — a multi-day wilderness approach to the Blue Glacier and West Peak, not a valley day hike.

name: Mt. Adams
whyNotable: Washington’s second-highest volcano, quieter than Rainier.
description: Washington’s second-highest volcano, a massive Cascade summit with broad snow slopes and quieter approaches than Rainier.

name: Denali
whyNotable: North America’s highest peak — cold, altitude, and multi-week expedition logistics.
description: Denali is a polar-altitude expedition, not a guided day climb. Most parties fly from Talkeetna to the Kahiltna and spend weeks on the West Buttress with sled hauling, cache management, and extreme cold. Register with Denali National Park, budget for weather delays, and treat acclimatization as the main objective.

name: Mt. Elbert
whyNotable: Colorado’s high point and the highest summit in the Rockies — a long walk-up with altitude.
description: Mount Elbert is a non-technical Sawatch Range walk-up and Colorado’s state high point. Standard North and South Mount Elbert trails are strenuous because of length and altitude, not scrambling. Stage from Leadville or Twin Lakes; start early for thunderstorms, and treat 14,000 ft as the main difficulty.

name: Mt. of the Holy Cross
whyNotable: Iconic Colorado 14er named for the snow cross on its northeast face.
description: A storied Sawatch 14er famous for the snow-filled cross couloir on its northeast face — a long Class 2 hike from Half Moon / Tigiwon approaches.

name: Mt. Massive
whyNotable: Second-highest peak in the Rocky Mountains; classic paired outing with Mt. Elbert.
description: Colorado’s second-highest summit and Elbert’s massive Sawatch neighbor — a long Class 2 ridge walk with broad alpine views above Leadville.

name: Mt. Harvard
whyNotable: Colorado’s third-highest summit and namesake of the Collegiate Peaks.
description: Third-highest peak in the Rockies — a long Class 2 hike from Horn Fork Basin near Buena Vista in the Collegiate Peaks.

name: Mt. Princeton
whyNotable: Prominent Collegiate Peaks 14er and a classic Buena Vista day hike.
description: A Collegiate Peaks 14er above Buena Vista — the popular East Slopes hike climbs from the radio towers road into alpine ridge terrain.

name: Mt. Yale
whyNotable: Popular Collegiate Peaks 14er with a classic Denny Creek approach.
description: A Collegiate Peaks 14er climbed via the Denny Creek / Southwest Slopes route — forest, then alpine, then a rocky Class 2 summit ridge.

name: Mt. Whitney
whyNotable: Highest peak in the contiguous U.S. — a long Class 1–2 trail with a hard permit quota.
description: Mount Whitney is a very long day or short overnight on the Mount Whitney Trail from Whitney Portal. The hiking is non-technical in summer, but altitude, distance, and a competitive Inyo National Forest permit quota stop more people than the terrain. Stage in Lone Pine; start early and respect afternoon Sierra weather.

name: White Mountain Peak
whyNotable: Third-highest peak in California; ultra-prominent White Mountains high point.
description: California’s third-highest summit and the high point of the White Mountains — a long high-desert ridge hike with expansive views toward the Sierra Nevada.

name: Boundary Peak
whyNotable: Highest peak in Nevada; sits on the California–Nevada border crest.
description: Nevada’s state high point on the California border — a rocky Class 2 scramble often approached with neighboring Montgomery Peak.

name: Half Dome
whyNotable: Yosemite’s cable-route icon — permit lottery, huge vertical, and seasonal cables.
description: Half Dome is a very strenuous Yosemite day (or overnight) via Mist Trail / John Muir Trail to the seasonal cable route. The cables turn the final slab into a secure scramble when up; without a cables permit you cannot proceed legally in season. Carry water, start early, and respect wet rock and afternoon storms.

name: El Capitan
whyNotable: World-famous Yosemite big wall; iconic American climbing landmark. Topographic prominence is only ~9 ft — it is a cliff shoulder, not an independent summit.
description: Yosemite’s sheer granite monolith — one of the world’s most famous big walls, rising nearly 3,000 feet above the Valley floor.

name: Mt. Tallac
whyNotable: One of Lake Tahoe’s most popular summit hikes with classic alpine-lake views.
description: Tahoe’s signature day-hike summit above Fallen Leaf Lake — a steep trail to panoramic views over Lake Tahoe and Desolation Wilderness.

name: Longs Peak
whyNotable: Front Range fourteener crowned by the famous Keyhole Route.
description: A classic Front Range fourteener in Rocky Mountain National Park, topped by the exposed Keyhole Route.

name: Grays Peak
whyNotable: Highest Continental Divide summit in Colorado; paired day hike with Torreys.
description: Highest peak on the Continental Divide in Colorado and a classic Front Range day outing, often paired with neighboring Torreys Peak.

name: Torreys Peak
whyNotable: Iconic paired 14er with Grays; one of Colorado’s most popular Front Range days.
description: Grays Peak’s twin on the Continental Divide — usually climbed together via the Grays/Torreys trail from Stevens Gulch.

name: Mt. Bierstadt
whyNotable: One of Colorado’s most accessible and heavily climbed beginner 14ers.
description: A popular beginner Colorado 14er above Guanella Pass — short approach, Class 2 West Slopes, and big views toward the Sawtooth and Mt. Evans.

name: Mount Blue Sky
whyNotable: One of Colorado’s most visited high summits — road-accessible 14er above the Denver Front Range.
description: Formerly Mt. Evans — a Front Range 14er with a seasonal summit highway and classic West Ridge hike from Summit Lake near Idaho Springs.

name: Pikes Peak
whyNotable: Colorado icon with a road, cog railway, and vast prairie views.
description: An iconic Front Range landmark above Colorado Springs, reachable by trail, cog railway, or the Pikes Peak Highway.

name: Quandary Peak
whyNotable: Among the most frequently summited Colorado 14ers; a classic day-hike introduction.
description: One of Colorado’s most climbed 14ers — a straightforward East Ridge hike from the Blue Lakes / Quandary trailhead near Breckenridge.

name: Mt. Sherman
whyNotable: A classic “first 14er” for many Colorado hikers thanks to a short approach and moderate ridge.
description: One of Colorado’s most accessible 14ers — a short Class 2 ridge hike from Fourmile Creek above Fairplay / Alma.

name: Gannett Peak
whyNotable: Wyoming’s high point, deep in the Wind River wilderness.
description: Wyoming’s high point in the remote Wind River Range, a glacier-guarded summit far from roads.

name: Granite Peak
whyNotable: Montana’s technical state high point in the Beartooths.
description: Montana’s high point in the Beartooth Mountains, a technical scramble on solid granite.

name: Borah Peak
whyNotable: Idaho state high point and a classic western Class 3 scramble.
description: Idaho’s high point — a steep Class 3 Chicken-Out Ridge scramble above Mackay with big Lost River Range exposure.

name: Kings Peak
whyNotable: Utah’s high point, a long Uintas backpack to the summit ridge.
description: Utah’s high point in the Uinta Mountains, a long alpine hike to the roof of the Beehive State.

name: Humphreys Peak
whyNotable: Arizona’s high point on the San Francisco Peaks volcanic field.
description: Arizona’s high point on the San Francisco Peaks, a forested volcanic summit near Flagstaff.

name: Guadalupe Peak
whyNotable: Texas high point rising abruptly from the Chihuahuan Desert.
description: Texas’s high point in Guadalupe Mountains National Park, rising abruptly above the Chihuahuan Desert.

name: Black Elk Peak
whyNotable: Highest peak in South Dakota; classic Black Hills fire-tower summit.
description: South Dakota’s high point (formerly Harney Peak) — a popular Black Hills hike to a stone fire tower with views across the plains.

name: Telescope Peak
whyNotable: Highest peak in Death Valley National Park; classic desert high-point hike.
description: Death Valley’s high point in the Panamint Range — a long desert ridge walk with views from Badwater Basin to Mount Whitney on clear days.

name: Mt. Robson
whyNotable: Canadian Rockies giant with one of the range’s biggest faces.
description: The highest peak in the Canadian Rockies, a steep ice-and-rock pyramid towering over Berg Lake.

name: Mt. Logan
whyNotable: Canada’s highest mountain, a vast Yukon ice massif.
description: Canada’s highest mountain and the largest base circumference of any non-volcanic peak on Earth, in Kluane’s icefields.

name: Mt. Waddington
whyNotable: British Columbia’s highest peak, remote Coast Range alpine.
description: The highest peak entirely in British Columbia, a remote Coast Mountains giant of ice and granite.

name: Mt. Columbia
whyNotable: Alberta’s high point on the Columbia Icefield divide.
description: A major Canadian Rockies summit on the Continental Divide, approached across the Columbia Icefield.

name: Mt. Assiniboine
whyNotable: The “Matterhorn of the Rockies,” a perfect pyramidal summit.
description: The “Matterhorn of the Rockies,” a striking pyramidal peak on the Alberta–British Columbia border.

name: Pico de Orizaba
whyNotable: Mexico’s highest peak and the tallest volcano in North America.
description: Mexico’s highest peak and North America’s third-highest, a massive stratovolcano often climbed via the Jamapa Glacier.

name: Popocatépetl
whyNotable: Mexico’s legendary smoking volcano above the Valley of Mexico.
description: An active Mexican volcano near Mexico City, historically climbed but often closed due to eruptive activity.

name: Aconcagua
whyNotable: Highest mountain outside Asia and the Andes’ great prize.
description: The highest mountain in the Western Hemisphere, a non-technical but punishing Andes giant in Argentina.

name: Huascarán
whyNotable: Peru’s high point and the crown of the Cordillera Blanca.
description: Peru’s high point in the Cordillera Blanca, a twin-summited ice giant and classic Andean expedition peak.

name: Illimani
whyNotable: The great ice pyramid watching over La Paz.
description: The great ice massif overlooking La Paz, a signature Cordillera Real climb with sweeping Altiplano views.

name: Chimborazo
whyNotable: The farthest point from Earth’s center due to equatorial bulge.
description: Ecuador’s highest volcano and, due to Earth’s equatorial bulge, the farthest point from the planet’s center.

name: Cotopaxi
whyNotable: One of the world’s highest active volcanoes, Ecuador’s icon.
description: One of the world’s highest active volcanoes, a near-perfect Ecuadorian cone and classic high-Andes climb.

name: Cerro Fitz Roy
whyNotable: Patagonia’s granite spire and a world-class alpine objective.
description: Patagonia’s granite spire icon, more often admired than climbed, rising above El Chaltén’s wind-scoured valleys.

name: Cerro Paine Grande
whyNotable: Highest summit in Torres del Paine National Park / Cordillera Paine — the famous towers sit nearby at lower elevations.
description: The high point of the Cordillera Paine massif in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile — a serious Patagonian objective above the iconic granite towers.

name: Sajama
whyNotable: Bolivia’s highest peak, a lonely volcano on the Altiplano.
description: Bolivia’s highest peak, an isolated Andean volcano on the Altiplano near the Chilean border.

name: Ausangate
whyNotable: Sacred Andean apu and the heart of Peru’s high circuit treks.
description: A sacred Apu of the Cordillera Vilcanota, ringed by the classic Ausangate circuit near Cusco.

name: Mont Blanc
whyNotable: The roof of the Alps and Western Europe’s highest summit.
description: Western Europe’s highest summit and the birthplace of modern alpinism, rising above Chamonix and Courmayeur.

name: Matterhorn
whyNotable: The world’s most famous alpine silhouette — a guided rock ridge, not a hike.
description: The Matterhorn’s Hörnli Ridge is a long alpine rock climb above Zermatt: fixed ropes, exposure, rockfall, and mandatory fitness for moving fast on a crowded route. Most parties hire a UIAGM guide and overnight at Hörnli Hut. No government summit permit—hut space and conditions are the real gates. Cervinia offers the Italian Lion Ridge approach.

name: Jungfrau
whyNotable: Bernese Oberland classic above the Jungfraujoch.
description: A Bernese Oberland classic above the Aletsch Glacier, long celebrated as one of the Alps’ great ice peaks.

name: Eiger
whyNotable: Infamous for its North Face, the Nordwand.
description: Bernese Alps legend defined by its North Face, a steep limestone wall that shaped twentieth-century climbing history.

name: Grossglockner
whyNotable: Austria’s highest mountain and an Eastern Alps landmark.
description: Austria’s highest mountain, a classic High Tauern ice climb above the Pasterze Glacier.

name: Triglav
whyNotable: Slovenia’s national mountain and a symbol of the Julian Alps.
description: Slovenia’s national mountain in the Julian Alps, a limestone ridge climb and cultural landmark.

name: Ortler
whyNotable: Highest peak in the Eastern Alps outside the Bernina.
description: The highest peak in the Eastern Alps of Italy, a glaciated Ortler Alps summit near South Tyrol.

name: Marmolada
whyNotable: Queen of the Dolomites, with a glacier and vast limestone walls.
description: The “Queen of the Dolomites,” a limestone massif with a remnant glacier and sweeping views over the Pale Mountains.

name: Barre des Écrins
whyNotable: High point of the Écrins and the southern French Alps.
description: The highest peak in the Dauphiné Alps of France, a remote Écrins massif climb of rock and ice.

name: Mt. Elbrus
whyNotable: Europe’s conventional high point on a twin-summited volcano.
description: Europe’s conventional high point, a twin-summited Caucasus volcano usually climbed via snow slopes from the south.

name: Mt. Kazbek
whyNotable: Georgia’s storied Caucasus giant above the Georgian Military Highway.
description: A sacred Caucasus volcano above Stepantsminda, combining glacier travel with Georgian mountain culture.

name: Damavand
whyNotable: Iran’s highest peak and the tallest volcano in Asia.
description: The highest volcano in Asia and Iran’s high point, a solitary Alborz cone rising above the Caspian hinterland.

name: Mt. Ararat
whyNotable: Turkey’s iconic twin-peaked volcano of legend and national identity.
description: A massive dormant volcano in eastern Turkey, culturally iconic and a long snow climb to its twin summits.

name: Kilimanjaro
whyNotable: Africa’s highest mountain — a non-technical trek to extreme altitude.
description: Africa’s highest mountain, a freestanding volcanic massif climbed by non-technical trekking routes to Uhuru Peak.

name: Mt. Kenya
whyNotable: Africa’s second-highest peak, technical rock above the treeline.
description: Africa’s second-highest peak, a rugged volcanic plug with technical summits above the equatorial moorlands.

name: Jebel Toubkal
whyNotable: Highest peak in North Africa and the Atlas Mountains.
description: North Africa’s high point in Morocco’s High Atlas, a popular scramble above the Imlil valley.

name: Ras Dashen
whyNotable: Ethiopia’s high point in the Simien Mountains massif.
description: Ethiopia’s high point in the Simien Mountains, a rocky plateau summit above dramatic escarpments.

name: Table Mountain
whyNotable: Cape Town’s flat-topped landmark and a World Heritage icon.
description: Cape Town’s flat-topped sandstone icon, more plateau than spire, and one of the world’s most recognizable city peaks.

name: Mt. Meru
whyNotable: Tanzania’s dramatic crater volcano and Kilimanjaro’s neighbor.
description: A steep volcanic neighbor of Kilimanjaro, often climbed as an acclimatization trek before Kibo.

name: Mt. Everest
whyNotable: Earth’s highest summit — permit-heavy, operator-driven, and season-critical.
description: Everest is a commercialized high-altitude expedition on the Nepal or Tibet side. Success depends on permits, a licensed operator, weather windows, and prior 8000 m experience more than summit-day fitness alone. Stage through Namche / Base Camp on the south side; budget for multiple agency fees and long logistics chains.

name: K2
whyNotable: The savage mountain — second highest, far more committing than Everest.
description: The savage mountain of the Karakoram — steeper, colder, and statistically more dangerous than Everest.

name: Kangchenjunga
whyNotable: The world’s third-highest peak, sacred and rarely summited for years.
description: The world’s third-highest mountain, a vast Himalayan massif sacred to communities of Sikkim and eastern Nepal.

name: Lhotse
whyNotable: Everest’s neighbor and the world’s fourth-highest mountain.
description: Everest’s towering southern neighbor, linked by the South Col and famous for the sheer Lhotse Face.

name: Makalu
whyNotable: A perfect pyramid and the world’s fifth-highest peak.
description: An isolated Mahalangur giant east of Everest, known for steep ridges and technical high-altitude climbing.

name: Cho Oyu
whyNotable: Often called the most “accessible” 8,000er — still extreme altitude.
description: The “Turquoise Goddess,” often considered the most attainable 8,000-meter peak via its northwest ridge.

name: Dhaulagiri
whyNotable: A vast white Himalayan wall and the world’s seventh-highest peak.
description: The White Mountain of west-central Nepal, an isolated 8,000er rising above the Kali Gandaki corridor.

name: Manaslu
whyNotable: The “mountain of the spirit,” Nepal’s classic 8,000er circuit peak.
description: Nepal’s “Mountain of the Spirit,” an 8,000-meter Mansiri Himal peak with a classic northeast face route.

name: Nanga Parbat
whyNotable: The western Himalaya’s killer mountain, famous for its Rupal Face.
description: The westernmost Himalayan giant, rising abruptly above the Indus with legendary Rupal and Diamir faces.

name: Annapurna I
whyNotable: First 8,000er climbed — still among the most dangerous.
description: The first 8,000-meter peak ever climbed, still among the most dangerous high mountains on Earth.

name: Gasherbrum I
whyNotable: Karakoram 8,000er known as Hidden Peak.
description: Hidden Peak of the Karakoram, an 8,000-meter neighbor of Broad Peak in the Gasherbrum group.

name: Broad Peak
whyNotable: A long summit ridge opposite K2 in the Karakoram.
description: A long Karakoram ridge peak beside K2, climbed via a classic snow-and-ice West Ridge style route.

name: Gasherbrum II
whyNotable: Often the “friendliest” Karakoram 8,000er — still serious.
description: Often the first Karakoram 8,000er for expedition climbers, a steep pyramid above the Baltoro Glacier.

name: Shishapangma
whyNotable: The only 8,000er entirely in Tibet / China.
description: The only 8,000-meter peak lying entirely in China/Tibet, long closed and later a popular Tibetan expedition.

name: Ama Dablam
whyNotable: Nepal’s “Matterhorn” — the most photographed Himalayan spire.
description: The “Matterhorn of the Himalaya,” a striking Khumbu spire more technical than many taller neighbors.

name: Island Peak
whyNotable: Classic Everest-region trekking peak and alpine intro.
description: Imja Tse, a popular Khumbu trekking peak used as an introduction to Himalayan glacier and rope travel.

name: Stok Kangri
whyNotable: Ladakh’s popular high trekking peak above the Indus Valley.
description: A popular Ladakh trekking peak near Leh, combining high altitude with a relatively accessible summit day.

name: Nanda Devi
whyNotable: India’s second-highest peak, once closed as a sacred sanctuary.
description: India’s second-highest peak, a sacred Garhwal sanctuary mountain long restricted after early expeditions.

name: Trisul
whyNotable: A striking Garhwal triple-summit massif near Nanda Devi.
description: A three-peaked Garhwal massif near Nanda Devi, historically significant in early Himalayan exploration.

name: Mt. Fuji
whyNotable: Japan’s sacred icon and busiest summit trail — seasonal fees and hut logistics matter.
description: Mount Fuji is a strenuous Class 1 volcano hike on crowded summer trails (Yoshida, Subashiri, Gotemba, Fujinomiya). Most climbers start from a 5th Station, overnight in a mountain hut, and aim for sunrise on the crater rim. Bring cash for huts/fees, expect cold wind at the rim, and avoid off-season attempts without winter skills.

name: Mt. Yari
whyNotable: The “Matterhorn of Japan” on the North Alps ridgeline.
description: The “Matterhorn of Japan” in the Northern Alps, a sharp ridgeline peak on classic hut-to-hut routes.

name: Hallasan
whyNotable: South Korea’s high point, a shield volcano crowning Jeju Island.
description: South Korea’s high point, a shield volcano forming Jeju Island with crater-lake trails to the summit.

name: Aoraki / Mt. Cook
whyNotable: New Zealand’s highest peak and the heart of the Southern Alps.
description: Aoraki, the highest peak in New Zealand, a glaciated Southern Alps icon above the Hooker and Tasman valleys.

name: Mt. Aspiring
whyNotable: The “Matterhorn of the South,” New Zealand’s classic alpine peak.
description: Tititea, the “Matterhorn of the South,” a elegant Southern Alps pyramid in Mount Aspiring National Park.

name: Mt. Tasman
whyNotable: New Zealand’s second-highest summit on the main divide.
description: New Zealand’s second-highest peak, a heavily glaciated neighbor of Aoraki on the Main Divide.

name: Mt. Kosciuszko
whyNotable: Australia’s high point — an accessible alpine walk in the Snowies.
description: Australia’s high point in the Snowy Mountains, a gentle alpine walk above Thredbo and Charlotte Pass.

name: Mt. Townsend
whyNotable: Often mistaken for Kosciuszko; Australia’s true runner-up summit.
description: Australia’s second-highest summit, a short alpine ridge away from Kosciuszko on the Main Range.

name: Galdhøpiggen
whyNotable: Northern Europe’s highest mountain, in Norway’s Jotunheimen.
description: Northern Europe’s highest mountain, a popular Jotunheimen hike with glacier and non-glacier approaches.

name: Kebnekaise
whyNotable: Sweden’s high point, with a shifting glacial summit.
description: Sweden’s high point in Lapland, a shifting glaciated summit above classic Arctic trail country.

name: Halti
whyNotable: Finland’s high point on the Norwegian border — a slope cairn (Hálditšohkka) with effectively zero topographic prominence; the taller Halti summit lies in Norway.
description: Finland’s country high point on the Halti fell, marked on the Norwegian border. The independent summit (Ráisduottarháldi) is about a kilometre into Norway.

name: Musala
whyNotable: The Balkans’ highest peak, in Bulgaria’s Rila Mountains.
description: The Balkan Peninsula’s highest peak in Bulgaria’s Rila Mountains, reached by marked alpine trails.

name: Mt. Olympus
whyNotable: Mythic home of the gods and Greece’s highest mountain.
description: Mythic home of the Greek gods, a rugged Olympus Massif climb to Mytikas above the Aegean foothills.

name: Mulhacén
whyNotable: Iberia’s highest peak, rising above the Sierra Nevada.
description: The Iberian Peninsula’s high point in Spain’s Sierra Nevada, a long alpine walk above Granada.

name: Teide
whyNotable: Spain’s highest mountain and a massive Atlantic volcano.
description: Spain’s highest peak and a towering Canary Islands volcano above Tenerife’s caldera landscapes.

name: Iztaccíhuatl
whyNotable: Alternate atlas entry for Mexico’s great ice volcano.
description: Iztaccíhuatl, the “White Woman” volcano beside Popocatépetl, a long snow ridge above the Valley of Mexico.

name: Illampu
whyNotable: A sharp Cordillera Real giant north of Lake Titicaca.
description: A steep Cordillera Real ice peak near Sorata, regarded as one of Bolivia’s more difficult high summits.

name: Alpamayo
whyNotable: Often called the world’s most beautiful mountain.
description: Often called the world’s most beautiful mountain, a fluted Cordillera Blanca pyramid of steep snow and ice.

name: Huayna Potosí
whyNotable: La Paz’s backyard 6,000er — a classic first big Andean climb.
description: A popular Cordillera Real training peak near La Paz, offering high-altitude glacier travel with hut access.

name: Mt. Vinson
whyNotable: Antarctica’s high point and a Seven Summits objective.
description: Mount Vinson, Antarctica’s high point in the Ellsworth Mountains, a remote polar expedition objective.

name: Mt. Sidley
whyNotable: Antarctica’s highest volcano, remote even by polar standards.
description: The highest volcano in Antarctica, a remote Executive Committee Range summit in Marie Byrd Land.

name: Mt. Mitchell
whyNotable: Highest peak east of the Mississippi in the U.S.
description: The highest peak east of the Mississippi, a forested Appalachian summit in North Carolina.

name: Kuwohi
whyNotable: Smokies high point and one of the most visited summits in the eastern United States.
description: The highest point in Great Smoky Mountains National Park (formerly Clingmans Dome) — a short paved path to the famous observation tower on the Tennessee–North Carolina crest.

name: Mt. LeConte
whyNotable: Among the most visited backcountry summits in the eastern U.S., with a historic summit lodge.
description: One of the Smokies’ most popular overnight destinations — Alum Cave and Rainbow Falls trails climb to LeConte Lodge and a forested summit complex.

name: Mt. Katahdin
whyNotable: Northern terminus of the Appalachian Trail in Maine.
description: Maine’s high point and the northern terminus of the Appalachian Trail, a rugged Baxter Peak above Knife Edge.

name: Cadillac Mountain
whyNotable: Acadia’s iconic summit and one of the most visited mountain viewpoints on the East Coast.
description: Acadia National Park’s high point and one of the first places to see sunrise in the U.S. — road- and trail-accessible granite summit above Bar Harbor.

name: Mt. Marcy
whyNotable: New York’s high point and the Adirondack crown.
description: New York’s high point in the Adirondacks, a long forest-and-alpine hike to the roof of the Empire State.

name: Mt. Mansfield
whyNotable: Highest peak in Vermont and the signature summit of the Green Mountains.
description: Vermont’s high point — a classic Long Trail / Forehead-to-Chin ridge hike above Stowe with alpine tundra and ski-area access.

name: Mt. Monadnock
whyNotable: Among the most frequently hiked peaks on Earth; classic New England summit.
description: One of the world’s most climbed mountains — a bare New Hampshire summit of open ledge trails above Jaffrey and Dublin.

name: Mt. Washington
whyNotable: Home to some of the world’s most extreme recorded weather.
description: The Northeast’s weather-extreme peak in New Hampshire’s Presidential Range, famous for alpine conditions.

name: Mt. Lafayette
whyNotable: Franconia Ridge high point; one of New England’s premier alpine day hikes.
description: The high point of Franconia Ridge — a classic White Mountains alpine traverse linking Little Haystack, Lincoln, and Lafayette above Franconia Notch.

name: Mt. Madison
whyNotable: Northern anchor of New Hampshire’s Presidential Range alpine crest.
description: Northernmost Presidential 5000-footer — rocky alpine trails above Madison Spring Hut on the classic Presidential Traverse.

name: Mt. Adams (NH)
whyNotable: Second-highest peak in New England; key Presidential Range alpine summit.
description: Second-highest peak in New England — a rugged Presidential summit of alpine rock between Madison and Jefferson on the Presidential Traverse.

name: Old Rag Mountain
whyNotable: One of the Mid-Atlantic’s most famous day hikes — a technical granite scramble in Shenandoah National Park.
description: Shenandoah’s legendary granite scramble — a permit-required circuit with rock slabs, chimneys, and huge Piedmont views near Sperryville.

name: Mt. Rogers
whyNotable: Highest peak in Virginia; Appalachian Trail destination near Grayson Highlands.
description: Virginia’s high point in the Mount Rogers massif — a spruce-fir Appalachian summit reached via the Appalachian Trail from Elk Garden or Grayson Highlands.

name: Mt. Timpanogos
whyNotable: Utah’s beloved Wasatch giant above Utah Valley.
description: A Wasatch Range classic above Utah Valley, a long ridge hike with cirques, wildflowers, and summit views.

name: Wheeler Peak
whyNotable: Nevada’s iconic Great Basin summit and one of the state’s highest peaks.
description: Great Basin National Park’s alpine high point — a long trail above bristlecone forests and Nevada’s scenic Snake Range crest.

name: Wheeler Peak
whyNotable: Highest point in New Mexico and a classic Taos alpine day hike.
description: New Mexico’s high point above Taos Ski Valley — a popular Williams Lake trail to an alpine summit in Carson National Forest.

name: Sandia Crest
whyNotable: The defining summit above Albuquerque and one of New Mexico’s most visited mountain destinations.
description: Albuquerque’s mountain skyline high point — road- and tram-accessible crest with La Luz and other Sandia Wilderness trails on the west face.

name: Lone Peak
whyNotable: A sharp granite Wasatch summit above Salt Lake’s southern ridge.
description: A sharp Wasatch granite summit above Salt Lake County, popular with scramblers and alpine climbers.

name: Grand Teton
whyNotable: The classic American alpine peak of the Teton Range.
description: The centerpiece of the Teton Range, a steep rock-and-snow climb above Jenny Lake and the Wyoming valley floor.

name: Mt. Moran
whyNotable: A broad Teton fortress above Jackson Lake.
description: A remote Teton massif known for long approaches and serious alpine rock routes above Jackson Lake.

name: Cloud Peak
whyNotable: High point of Wyoming’s Bighorn Mountains wilderness.
description: The high point of Wyoming’s Bighorn Mountains, a wilderness scramble above glacier-carved basins.

name: Blanca Peak
whyNotable: Monarch of the Sangre de Cristo and a sacred Navajo peak.
description: The monarch of the Sangre de Cristo, a high Colorado fourteener above the San Luis Valley.

name: Crestone Peak
whyNotable: A rugged Colorado fourteener in the Crestone group.
description: A rugged Sangre de Cristo fourteener, often linked with Crestone Needle on classic Colorado ridge days.

name: Crestone Needle
whyNotable: One of Colorado’s most striking 14ers; often linked with Crestone Peak.
description: A sharp Sangre de Cristo 14er beside Crestone Peak — classic Class 3 scrambling on solid rock via Ellingwood Arete or the standard South Face.

name: Capitol Peak
whyNotable: Colorado’s knife-edge fourteener near Aspen.
description: An Elk Mountains knife-edge classic near Aspen, one of Colorado’s more committing fourteeners.

name: Pyramid Peak
whyNotable: A steep Elk Mountains fourteener above Maroon Creek.
description: A steep Elk Mountains fourteener above Maroon Creek, known for loose rock and exposed summit ridges.

name: Maroon Peak
whyNotable: Postcard Maroon Bells summit; among Colorado’s most iconic Elk Mountain 14ers.
description: The higher Maroon Bell — a Class 3 South Ridge classic above Maroon Lake and one of Colorado’s most photographed mountain pairs.

name: Mt. Sneffels
whyNotable: One of Colorado’s most photographed 14ers and a classic Ouray / Ridgway objective.
description: Iconic San Juan 14er above Yankee Boy Basin — a steep Class 3 scramble with classic Colorado “Matterhorn” summit views near Ouray.

name: Uncompahgre Peak
whyNotable: San Juan Mountains high point and one of Colorado’s most prominent 14ers.
description: Highest peak in the San Juans — a broad Class 2 summit hike from Nellie Creek with huge views above Lake City.

name: Handies Peak
whyNotable: Among the most accessible San Juan 14ers; classic American Basin day hike.
description: One of Colorado’s easier San Juan 14ers — a Class 1–2 hike from American Basin or Grizzly Gulch with broad alpine meadows and big views.

name: Mauna Kea
firstAscent: Ancient Hawaiian; first recorded European ascent 1823
bestSeason: Year-round; summit can be cold or snowy in winter
whyNotable: Tallest mountain on Earth measured from ocean floor to summit, and one of the world’s great astronomy sites.
description: Hawaii Island’s high shield volcano and a premier astronomy summit, rising above the Pacific with alpine cinder cones and rare snow on tropical latitudes.

name: Mauna Loa
whyNotable: Largest volcano on Earth by volume; active Hawaiian shield beside Mauna Kea.
description: Earth’s largest shield volcano by volume — a vast, gently sloping Hawaiian giant beside Mauna Kea, with long alpine approaches above the rainforest.

name: Haleakalā
whyNotable: Maui’s iconic volcano and one of Hawaii’s most visited national-park summits.
description: Maui’s shield-volcano high point and Haleakalā National Park’s summit — road-accessible crater rim with Sliding Sands and Halemauʻu wilderness trails into the crater.

name: Mt. St. Helens
bestSeason: Late spring–early fall for summit climbs
whyNotable: The 1980 eruption reshaped the mountain and made it a living laboratory of volcanic recovery.
description: A Cascade stratovolcano remade by the 1980 eruption, with a breached crater, lava dome, and recovering forests around Spirit Lake.

name: Monte Rosa (Dufourspitze)
whyNotable: Highest summit in Switzerland and second-highest in the Alps after Mont Blanc.
description: The Dufourspitze crowns the Monte Rosa massif on the Swiss–Italian border above Zermatt and Macugnaga. Standard approaches are long glacier climbs with crevasse hazard and high-camp logistics from the Monte Rosa Hut or Italian bivouacs. Treat it as a serious Pennine Alps expedition peak, not a day hike.

name: Weisshorn
whyNotable: One of the great isolated 4000ers of the Valais — a steep pyramid above Randa.
description: The Weisshorn is a classic Valais 4000er: long approaches, mixed rock and snow ridges, and serious exposure on the standard East Ridge from the Weisshorn Hut. Most parties treat it as a guided or highly experienced alpine climb from Randa / Täsch.

name: Dom
whyNotable: Highest mountain entirely in Switzerland — the Mischabel giant above Saas-Fee.
description: The Dom is the highest peak lying wholly in Switzerland, rising from the Mischabel range above Saas-Fee. The Festigrat / normal route is a long glacier climb from the Dom Hut with sustained altitude and crevasse terrain. Stage in Saas-Fee and budget for an alpine start.

name: Dent Blanche
whyNotable: Striking Valais rock pyramid guarding the approaches between Zinal and Zermatt.
description: Dent Blanche is a sharp Pennine Alps pyramid climbed most often via the South Ridge (Wandfluegrat) from the Dent Blanche Hut. Expect sustained rock, snow patches, and route-finding in mixed terrain. Stage from Les Haudères / Evolène or Zermatt-side valleys.

name: Piz Bernina
whyNotable: Easternmost 4000er of the Alps — the Bernina high point above Pontresina.
description: Piz Bernina is the highest summit of the Eastern Alps and the easternmost Alpine 4000er. The normal Spallagrat / Biancograt approaches from Diavolezza or the Tschierva Hut combine glacier travel with an airy final ridge. Stage in Pontresina or St. Moritz.

name: Gran Paradiso
whyNotable: Highest peak entirely in Italy — the classic first 4000er of the Graian Alps.
description: Gran Paradiso is Italy’s highest mountain wholly inside the country and a popular first 4000er. The normal route from Rifugio Vittorio Emanuele II is a glacier climb to a short final scramble on the Madonna summit block. Stage in Valsavarenche (Aosta Valley) inside Gran Paradiso National Park.

name: Cima Grande di Lavaredo
whyNotable: The highest of the Tre Cime / Drei Zinnen — the postcard wall of the Dolomites.
description: Cima Grande is the central and highest tower of the Tre Cime di Lavaredo. The normal route is a classic Dolomite rock climb with fixed gear in places; the north face holds historic hard routes. Most visitors hike the circuit around the towers from Rifugio Auronzo without summiting.

name: Ben Nevis
whyNotable: Highest mountain in the British Isles — Scotland’s classic summit walk.
description: Ben Nevis is the highest peak in the UK. The Mountain Track (pony track) from Glen Nevis is a long, steep day hike in all weather; the North Face holds serious winter and rock climbs. Navigation errors in cloud are common—carry a map/compass and turn around if conditions collapse.

name: Snowdon / Yr Wyddfa
whyNotable: Highest peak in Wales — busy ridge walks and a summit café above Llanberis.
description: Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) is Wales’s high point and one of Britain’s busiest mountains. Popular paths include Llanberis, Pyg, Miners, Watkin, and Rhyd Ddu; Crib Goch adds exposed scrambling. Trains on the Snowdon Mountain Railway also reach the summit complex in season.

name: Scafell Pike
whyNotable: Highest mountain in England — the Lake District’s rocky high point.
description: Scafell Pike is England’s highest summit. The Corridor Route from Wasdale or approaches from Seathwaite / Borrowdale are rocky, eroded day hikes with frequent cloud and navigation traps. Pair with Great Gable or Scafell only if daylight and skills allow.

name: Carrauntoohil
whyNotable: Highest mountain in Ireland — the Reeks horseshoe above the Hag’s Glen.
description: Carrauntoohil is Ireland’s high point in MacGillycuddy’s Reeks, County Kerry. The Brother O’Shea’s Gully / Devil’s Ladder approaches from Cronin’s Yard involve steep loose ground and frequent cloud; the Reeks Ridge is a serious scramble outing. Stage near Killarney or Beaufort.

name: Gerlachovský štít
whyNotable: Highest peak in the High Tatras and of Slovakia — guide-required for most visitors.
description: Gerlachovský štít is the high point of the High Tatras and Slovakia. The normal routes are technical enough that unguided ascent is restricted for visitors without local alpine qualifications—most hire a UIMLA/IFMGA mountain guide from Starý Smokovec or Tatranská Lomnica.

name: Mount Etna
whyNotable: Europe’s highest and most active volcano — Sicily’s restless summit.
description: Mount Etna is Europe’s tallest active volcano. Summit elevation changes with eruptions; cableways and 4×4 tours from Rifugio Sapienza or Piano Provenzana shorten approaches, but crater-rim travel depends on volcanic alert levels. Always check INGV / park closures before going high.

name: Mount Vesuvius
whyNotable: The volcano that buried Pompeii — a short crater-rim walk above the Bay of Naples.
description: Vesuvius is the iconic volcano overlooking Naples and the site of the 79 AD eruption that buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. Today a ticketed path reaches the crater rim on a short, steep walk. Check park opening hours and volcanic alert status; summer heat and crowds are intense.

name: Slide Mountain
whyNotable: Highest peak in the Catskills and the high point of Ulster County and the New York metro area.
description: Slide Mountain anchors the Burroughs Range in Catskill Park. The Wittenberg–Cornell–Slide Trail is the classic approach—a long forest hike with ledge views near the top. The true summit is wooded; ledges and openings nearby give the best vistas. Expect mud, roots, and busy weekends in leaf season.

name: Hunter Mountain
whyNotable: Second-highest Catskill peak, topped by a restored fire tower with wide views over the range.
description: Hunter Mountain rises above the village of Hunter in Greene County. Hikers reach the fire-tower summit via Becker Hollow, Spruceton, or ski-area connectors. Winter brings deep snow and wind on the open tower; summer weekends are busy. The ski resort occupies the north face—stay on designated hiking routes.

name: Black Dome
whyNotable: Third-highest Catskill peak and the high point of the Blackhead Range above Big Hollow.
description: Black Dome sits between Thomas Cole and Blackhead on the Blackhead Range. The Black Dome Range Trail links the trio; most hikers stage from Big Hollow Road. Expect steep forest climbs, muddy cols, and limited summit views through the trees—better vistas open on ledges along the ridge.

name: Blackhead
whyNotable: Eastern pillar of the Blackhead Range and one of four Catskill 3500 Club required winter peaks.
description: Blackhead anchors the east end of the Blackhead Range and sits on the Escarpment / Long Path corridor. Approaches from Big Hollow or the Escarpment are steep; the eastern pitch can hold ice well into spring. Summit views are limited, but lookouts along the ridge open toward the Hudson Valley.

name: West Kill Mountain
whyNotable: High point of the Devil’s Path west of Stony Clove—steep, rooty, and classic Catskills ridge hiking.
description: West Kill Mountain is the western crown of the Devil’s Path above Spruceton Valley. The Diamond Notch / Devil’s Path approach is steep and often wet, with Buck Ridge Lookout as the signature viewpoint. Expect a full day, scarce water on the ridge, and quieter crowds than Slide or Hunter.
